analysis.tldr: If the Reserve Bank of India (India's central bank that controls interest rates) raises interest rates as expected, loans for homes and cars could become more expensive.
the_story: A Union Bank of India report says the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) is expected to raise the repo rate (the interest rate at which the central bank lends money to commercial banks) by 25 basis points (0.25 percentage points) in October.
The report suggests one or two more rate hikes could happen in the financial year 2027.
These combined moves could take the benchmark rate (the standard interest rate that guides all other borrowing costs in the economy) up to 5.75% to 6%.
The report also notes that G-Sec yields (the interest rate the government pays to borrow money by issuing bonds) face upward pressure.
analysis.what_happened: A research report from the Union Bank of India predicts that the RBI will increase its main lending rate in October and possibly again later in FY27. This happens when analysts expect the central bank to tighten monetary policy, which usually occurs to keep prices stable or control inflation.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local bank slowly raising the rent on its money because demand for loans is shifting, meaning anyone wanting to borrow has to pay a higher price.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI is predicted to raise the repo rate (the interest rate banks pay to borrow from the central bank).
Commercial banks will pass these higher borrowing costs onto regular customers.
This pushes up interest rates on retail loans like home and car loans, making EMIs (monthly loan payments) higher for everyday borrowers.
At the same time, government bond yields face upward pressure, meaning the government has to pay higher interest when it borrows money.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Higher expected interest rates put upward pressure on yields, which is bad for the government as its borrowing costs go up.
When the repo rate climbs, banks make loans costlier, meaning higher monthly EMIs for people buying homes or cars — generally bad for borrowers.
Banks often raise rates on fixed deposits to attract savings when overall interest rates go up — which is good for savers.

analysis.caveats: The text was very short and largely made up of a mix of unrelated headline snippets and a single bank report prediction that may not happen if economic conditions change.

events.article_text:

RFE/RL journalists report the news in 21 countries where a free press is banned by the government or not fully established. We provide what many…

The flow of crude from the Persian Gulf has recovered to near-prewar levels, but the latest data shows that much of the oil is reaching markets through routes and shipping arrangements that did not exist before the war, raising the question of whether Iran is losing its leverage in the Strait of Hormuz.

At least 16.5 million barrels per day of crude left the region between September 1 and 28, matching the prewar average when Iran is excluded, according to commodity analytics firm Kpler.

But while crude levels have risen, the refinery bottleneck that has caused a global spike in diesel prices persists. European Union figures published on October 1 showed diesel pump prices at record levels. Prices have also surged in the United States despite the recovery in oil exports.

The route, meanwhile, has changed dramatically.

Before the war, 83 percent of the region's crude crossed the Strait of Hormuz. In September, 40 percent bypassed the strait, with oil instead moving through pipelines and other routes via Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. About 60 percent, or 9.9 million barrels per day, physically crossed Hormuz.

Kpler said more than 70 percent of the crude that crossed the strait in August -- the most recent month available -- changed tankers offshore in the Gulf of Oman, highlighting how far the current system is from normal commercial shipping.

For Iran, the recovery is a sign that its ability to disrupt the waterway has been significantly degraded.

Mohammad Ghaedi, a lecturer at George Washington University, told RFE/RL's Radio Farda that the current level of traffic was already too much for Tehran and "unacceptable" to authorities there.

But the figures do not mean Iran has simply lost control of Hormuz. Tehran never formally controlled the strait in the first place. Its leverage has instead rested on its ability to make the passage dangerous, forcing shipping companies to weigh the risks and costs of entering the Gulf.

That ability appears to have weakened as US forces provide protection for commercial shipping and companies develop ways to move oil while limiting their exposure to the strait.

Ellen R. Wald, author and energy markets analyst, told RFE/RL that Iran's "ability and/or will to attack ships in the Gulf is declining," allowing vessels to transit under US military cover.

But she cautioned that the recovery in flows should not be mistaken for a return to normalcy.

Some shipping companies are accepting significant risks to effectively ferry oil through the strait to larger tankers waiting outside the Gulf. Others are operating without insurance or under unusually difficult conditions.

"This is not a return to normal," Wald said. "These are significant risks and come with high costs."

And that is why oil prices aren't dropping much despite oil flows increasing.

The rebound in crude flows has reduced some of the immediate pressure on global supplies, but Wald does not expect oil prices to return to prewar levels yet. The continued threat to vessels, elevated insurance costs, and dependence on US military protection mean that a "war premium" remains embedded in the price of oil.

The latest Kpler figures also show why the recovery in exports should not be confused with the restoration of the old Gulf oil-trading system.

Before the war, almost all of the region's crude exports depended on Hormuz. Now, pipelines, Red Sea routes, and offshore ship-to-ship transfers are helping producers circumvent the chokepoint. Kpler said the region's export system has effectively been rebuilt around the disruption.

The more oil that moves without being stopped, the weaker Tehran's ability to use Hormuz as a coercive tool becomes. But the extraordinary measures required to keep that oil moving also demonstrate that the strait remains a source of leverage.

Ghaedi said he does not believe Iran is likely to attack regional energy infrastructure, despite commentary from Tehran that it could escalate by targeting oil facilities. He argued that reports portraying Iran as having lost control of Hormuz could themselves risk provoking such a response.

For now, however, the evidence points to a gradual erosion rather than a complete disappearance of Iranian leverage. And as long as ships still require military protection, unusual routing and costly workarounds to move that oil, Hormuz remains a vulnerability for Washington, even if Iran is no longer able to exercise the same degree of pressure over it that it did at the height of the war.

the_story: Crude oil flow from the Persian Gulf recovered to near-prewar levels between September 1 and 28, with at least 16.5 million barrels per day leaving the region, according to data from Kpler.

The shipping routes have changed drastically: before the war, 83% of the region's crude crossed the Strait of Hormuz, but in September, 40% bypassed it using pipelines through Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

Iran's leverage is weakening because US forces are protecting commercial ships and companies are finding alternative routes, though shipping companies are still taking on high risks, insurance costs, and offshore ship-to-ship transfers.

Despite higher oil exports, global diesel pump prices remain at record levels in the European Union and have surged in the US because refinery bottlenecks and a 'war premium' (extra cost added by risks and danger) remain embedded in prices.
analysis.what_happened: Oil shipments from the Middle East have bounced back to near-prewar levels (16.5 million barrels per day in September) because countries and companies found clever workarounds like pipelines through Saudi Arabia and the UAE, bypassing the dangerous Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, US military protection is helping commercial ships move through the area, weakening Iran's ability to disrupt the waterway.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major highway getting blocked by trouble, so delivery trucks are forced to take expensive detours through bumpy backroads. Even though goods are finally arriving, the extra fuel and danger mean shop prices stay stubbornly high.
why_it_matters_india: Middle East oil supply bottlenecks and workarounds keep global oil prices sticky and elevated due to high insurance and shipping costs.

Costlier imported energy feeds directly into domestic inflation (rising prices of everyday goods), making transport, manufacturing, and household items more expensive.

impacts.rationale: High shipping risks and refinery bottlenecks mean global fuel prices stay elevated, which is bad for everyday vehicle owners and transport costs.
Costlier fuel and transport expenses push up the prices of daily goods and services, which is bad for household budgets.

items.title: RBI backs blockchain technology, remains cautious on crypto: Guv Malhotra
items.summary: India has maintained a cautious approach towards cryptocurrencies while promoting the underlying technologies such as distributed ledger technology and tokenisation, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said on Saturday. events.article_text:
RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra | Image: Bloomberg

India has maintained a cautious approach towards cryptocurrencies while promoting the underlying technologies such as distributed ledger technology and tokenisation, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said on Saturday.

Malhotra said India supports innovation in technologies underlying crypto assets, including distributed ledger and tokenisation, but remains cautious about cryptocurrencies due to concerns over monetary sovereignty, monetary policy and capital flows.

"So, our approach has been to promote the underlying technologies, and we are using some of these in the central bank and outside in PPP (public-private partnership) mode. But insofar as crypto is concerned, it has been a cautious approach," he said at the Kautilya Economic Conclave.

Expressing concerns about cryptocurrencies, the RBI Governor said it is related to the 'singleness of money' and their potential implications for monetary policy, particularly in emerging market economies, where capital flow restrictions are in place.

"The problem that you are trying to address is primarily not so much of domestic payments, because domestic payments within our country and in many countries now are quite fast, cheap and convenient," he said.

The more significant challenge is cross-border payments, for which other solutions, including central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), can be explored, he said.

On rising public debt and hardening bond yields globally, Malhotra said the yield movement is essentially a function of demand and supply, with government and private-sector spending rising, including on account of artificial intelligence (AI).

"Money is scarce, spending has increased, both by the government as well as private enterprises, led by AI, and so that's what is leading to the hardening of the bond yields and debts," he said.

Malhotra said the RBI's monetary policy primarily focuses on domestic growth-inflation dynamics. But global interest rates also have implications for India, including through their impact on real interest rates in the country.

"That is something that we need to take care of," he said.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

analysis.tldr: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI, the central bank that manages the country's money) will keep strict rules on private cryptocurrencies to protect the economy, while using their underlying digital technology for official projects.
the_story: RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra stated on Saturday that India supports technologies behind crypto—like distributed ledger technology (a shared digital database) and tokenisation (converting asset rights into digital tokens)—while staying cautious about cryptocurrencies.

The RBI is concerned that private cryptocurrencies threaten the 'singleness of money' (the idea that all money in a country must hold equal, trusted value) and could disrupt monetary policy (the central bank's control over money supply and interest rates) and capital flows.
Malhotra noted that domestic digital payments in India are already fast, cheap, and convenient, meaning crypto is not needed for local transactions.

For cross-border payments (sending money across international borders), Malhotra suggested exploring other solutions like Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs, official digital money issued by a central bank).

On global financial matters, Malhotra explained that rising government and private-sector spending—especially driven by investments in artificial intelligence (AI)—is making money scarce and hardening bond yields (pushing up the interest rates governments pay when they borrow money) globally.
analysis.what_happened: RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra explained India's official stance at the Kautilya Economic Conclave. He separated private cryptocurrencies—which the central bank worries could harm the country's financial stability and money control—from their underlying technologies like distributed ledgers and tokenisation, which the RBI actively promotes through public-private partnerships.
analysis.analogy: It is like a government banning unofficial, homemade currency notes because they are risky, while taking the high-tech security paper and printing presses used to make them and using them to build a safer, official digital rupee.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI remains firmly opposed to speculative private cryptocurrencies, preventing them from becoming mainstream money in India.
Instead, the central bank is leaning into official digital currency solutions like CBDCs and public-private partnerships to improve cross-border payments.
Globally, heavy spending on artificial intelligence and rising government debt are pushing up bond yields worldwide.
Because global interest rates affect India, the RBI must carefully balance these outside pressures alongside domestic growth and inflation.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Global money is becoming scarcer as governments and AI-led companies borrow more, which pushes up borrowing costs worldwide, meaning higher loan costs for the Indian government—bad for public finances.

impacts.target: India's inflation rate (the speed at which everyday prices rise)
impacts.rationale: Global cost pressures and hardening yields can leak into the domestic economy, making imported goods pricier—bad for household budgets.

watch_next: Updates from the RBI on the rollout and adoption of Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs)
Global trends in artificial intelligence spending and international bond yields
analysis.caveats: Global spending on artificial intelligence and rising public debt could change course faster or slower than anticipated, altering the path of global bond yields.

events.headline: African nations begin to stock up rice on El Nino fears, Ukraine and Iran wars

items.title: African nations begin to stock up rice on El Nino fears, Ukraine and Iran wars
items.summary: Ships are waiting to load rice consignments in almost all Indian ports, say exporters

events.article_text:
African countries are building rice inventories to face any challenge that a severe El Nino and the geopolitical situation could pose by buying more of the cereal from India. This has lifted rice prices in the global market, with Indian rice prices increasing by 20 per cent over the past few months.

“African nations are buying more to create a buffer. I have never seen a situation like now, when 20 vessels have anchored at one time in Kakinada that can ship six lakh tonnes,” said New Delhi-based exporter Rajesh Paharia Jain.

“Ships are waiting to lift rice in almost all ports. There are two reasons. One is El Nino. The other is the Ukraine and Iran wars. Fears of food security have gripped the world. Some countries are buying double the quantity they usually purchase,” said Suraj Agarwal, Vice-President (West Bengal), Indian Rice Exporters Federation.

However, Mukesh Jain, President, The Rice Exporters Association, Chhattisgarh, said some of the exporters are fulfilling earlier contracts as there has been a delay in shipments due to the Iran war.

But there could be a temporary setback as Vietnam is facing problems in exporting to the Philippines. Madan Prakash, President of Tamil Nadu Agri Commodities Exporters Association, said the situation has changed over the past couple of days with Indian ships laden with rice being stranded in Vietnam.

“Manila has stopped imports and Hanoi has been affected badly. In turn, they have now left Indian ships that have reached Vietnam stranded mid-sea. Prices of Vietnamese rice have dropped. It could happen to rice from other countries too,” Prakash, who is in Vietnam currently, said over the phone.

“When we started exports in May, prices were $335 a tonne f.o.b (free on-board) for 5 per cent broken parboiled rice. Today, no one is offering below $390,” said Paharia Jain.

“The problem with rice exports is more due to high freight rates. Freight charges per container have increased from $100 to $5,000 for consignments to Jebel Ali from Mumbai,” said Agarwal.

Ships are now anchoring at Khor Fakkan port, which is small. As a result, there is a huge buildup of waiting vessels. A shipment which took 5 days to a week to Jebel Ali now takes a month, he said.

“Indian rice prices have increased because freight rates have soared. We expect demand due to El Nino to emerge only later,” said Mukesh Jain.

Agarwal said the supply chain has been disturbed by India’s south-west monsoon, which has led to delayed rain in some areas, deficient rainfall in some, excess precipitation in some and unseasonal showers in other areas.

“It has affected the production of rice in some parts,” he said.

Paharia Jain said rice production could be lower by at least 10 per cent compared with last year. “Production of premium non-basmati could be badly affected,” he said.

Last year, India produced a record high of 124.5 million tonnes of rice during the kharif season. This year, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana have reported a sharp fall in the coverage.

“Storage in some reservoirs is worrisome in a few States. For example, Karnataka has said it will not release water for rabi crops and is saving it for drinking purposes,” said Agarwal.

As a result, prices of Sona Masuri have increased to ₹58-59 a kg from ₹45-46, while Swarna Masuri, one of the cheapest varieties, costs ₹36 against ₹31-32 a few months ago, he said.

Mukesh Jain said exporters are paying ₹2,450 a quintal for IR64 rice, which is higher than the minimum support price of ₹2,441 for common rice this crop year to June 2027.

Data from the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) show that rice exports during April-July of the current fiscal increased to 5.40 million tonnes, valued at $1.97 billion, compared with 4.48 million tonnes valued at $1.87 billion in the same period a year ago.

Agarwal said India need not worry in case of weather affecting rabi rice production too, as it had stocks that are a 5-year high. Data from the Food Corporation of India show that as of mid-September, India had 39.1 million tonnes of rice and 30.75 million tonnes of paddy, which could yield 20.6 million tonnes of rice.

“With the stocks we have, we can feed rice to the whole world for two years,” he said.

Paharia Jain said India could export 22-23 million tonnes of rice, including Basmati, during the current fiscal. “It could even touch 24 million tonnes if El Nino tends to be too harsh,” he said.

The development comes on the heels of India’s External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar warning of a major food crisis in the coming months, particularly due to the Ukraine war, which has affecting shipping in the Black Sea region, and Iran war.

events.headline: Australia and India need a treaty and a trade deal

items.title: Australia and India need a treaty and a trade deal
items.summary: A bilateral investment treaty can protect Australian capital in India, an economic cooperation agreement must make the resulting businesses viable.

events.article_text:
A bilateral investment treaty can protect Australian capital in India, an economic cooperation agreement must make the resulting businesses viable.

Australia and India need a treaty and a trade deal

On 25 September, Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said Australia and India were pursuing a bilateral investment treaty (Opens in new window) (BIT), alongside a comprehensive economic cooperation agreement (CECA). These negotiations reopen an unfinished question: how can the two countries protect investment while helping their businesses produce together?

The BIT should provide credible protection for capital; CECA should make the resulting businesses viable. That means connecting Australian resources, processing, and technology with Indian manufacturing, under rules that allow both countries to gain capabilities and commercial returns.

The Sicona–Himadri partnership (Opens in new window) shows the possibilities. In May 2025, Himadri committed A$15 million to Wollongong battery company Sicona alongside a licence to manufacture its silicon-carbon anode technology in India. Indian capital would support Australian pilot operations; Indian production offered prospective royalties. Each country could benefit from the other’s industrial development.

The rules protecting such investments have changed. The 1999 Agreement on the Promotion and Protection of Investments (Opens in new window), effective from May 2000, promised fair and equitable treatment, compensation for expropriation, and transfers of investment funds. It also allowed investors to bring claims against the host government through international arbitration. These were enforceable commitments about how capital would be treated.

The challenge is that both governments want more production at home.

The consequences became clear in 2011, when Australian company White Industries won a claim (Opens in new window) against India after Indian courts took nine years to resolve efforts to enforce a commercial arbitration award. A clause promising treatment no less favourable than that given to third-country investors allowed the tribunal to draw stronger protection for legal remedies from India’s treaty with Kuwait. India’s Law Commission later linked (Opens in new window) this award and other investor claims to the rethink of its treaty program.

India’s government argued (Opens in new window) that older treaty language invited broad and ambiguous interpretations. Its revised model, approved in December 2015, generally required investors to pursue domestic remedies, for at least five years, before arbitration and excluded areas including taxation, subsidies, and procurement. India then moved to terminate and renegotiate older agreements (Opens in new window). Ending the Australian treaty was part of that wider policy overhaul.

The legacy remains. Termination took effect on 23 March 2017 (Opens in new window), but a fifteen-year survival clause preserves protection for eligible investments made before that date until March 2032. Later investments cannot rely on the old treaty. Domestic law and contractual rights remain available, but investors have different bilateral treaty protections depending on when they invested. For a new factory, that changes the remedies available if government action harms the investment. A replacement must address that gap.

Doing so requires credible remedies alongside clear protection for legitimate regulation. Australia also opposes investor–state arbitration in new trade agreements (Opens in new window), making enforcement a central negotiating question. The new treaty should define investor rights, regulatory exceptions, and dispute procedures precisely. But even sound protections cannot guarantee customers, product approvals, or eligibility for industrial support. That is where CECA becomes essential.

Sideline talks in July during ASEAN meetings between Indian External Affairs Minister Dr S. Jaishankar and Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong (Daniel Walding/DFAT)

The challenge is that both governments want more production at home. Australia’s critical minerals tax incentive (Opens in new window) will support eligible domestic processing from July 2027. India’s advanced chemistry cell incentive (Opens in new window) requires 60% domestic value addition within five years. Shared strategic interests therefore coexist with potentially competing preferences over where factories and jobs should be located.

Tariff preferences do not settle that competition. Under the existing Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement (ECTA), Australian-originating inputs (Opens in new window) used in Indian production can count towards bilateral origin, but not automatically towards Indian domestic content under an incentive scheme. India’s procurement rules (Opens in new window) also ordinarily exclude overseas royalties from local-content calculations. A product can qualify for lower tariffs while its producer faces separate tests for subsidies or public contracts.

Even a qualifying product still needs regulatory approval. ECTA provides for acceptance of the other country’s testing and certification results (Opens in new window) only “whenever possible”, subject to equivalent assurance. Investors must therefore establish both whether their products receive preferential treatment and whether they can reach customers.

CECA should tackle these conditions together, using prospective battery and minerals projects to identify practical obstacles. It should clarify the production steps and imported inputs that qualify goods for tariff preferences. With procurement already under negotiation (Opens in new window), governments should specify covered buyers, products, and treatment of jointly produced goods. Changes to manufacturing-incentive eligibility require separate, explicit commitments.

analysis.tldr: Australia and India are working on a new investment treaty and trade deal to help businesses build things together, but they still need to figure out how to solve disputes and handle local manufacturing rules.
the_story: On 25 September, Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said Australia and India are pursuing a bilateral investment treaty (an agreement between two countries to protect cross-border investments) alongside a comprehensive economic cooperation agreement (a broad trade and economic deal).

The Sicona–Himadri partnership illustrates the potential: in May 2025, India's Himadri committed A$15 million to Australian battery company Sicona for a licence to manufacture its silicon-carbon anode technology in India.

India terminated its older 1999 investment treaty with Australia in March 2017 (ending in full by March 2032 due to a survival clause) after legal disputes like the 2011 White Industries case led India to require investors to use local courts first.

Both governments want more production at home, creating competition over jobs and factories, underscored by Australia's critical minerals tax incentive starting July 2027 and India's requirement for 60% domestic value addition for advanced chemistry cells.

Current tariff preferences under the Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement do not automatically solve local-content rules for subsidies or public procurement, meaning a trade deal alone cannot guarantee market access or factory success.
analysis.what_happened: India and Australia are negotiating a new investment treaty and trade deal to replace an older pact that India cancelled in 2017. The talks aim to bridge differences over how to protect business investments and handle disputes, while both countries push to boost domestic manufacturing.
analysis.analogy: It is like two business partners trying to write new rules for sharing a kitchen, where both want to make sure their own local cooks get the most jobs.

Partnerships like the Himadri-Sicona battery venture test how joint production works in practice.

items.title: A new contest pits competitors against each other in a race to biological youth
items.summary: This week, I officially signed up for an unusual competition. One that rewards competitors for getting younger. events.article_text:
This week, I officially signed up for an unusual competition. One that rewards competitors for getting younger.

I recently turned 40, and I don’t need reminding that both time and my chronological age only tick forward. But this game is focused on competitors’ biological ages—figures that are meant to provide a better way to measure the age-related health of our organs and bodies.

Over a six-month period, around 500 of us will try to reverse our biological age as measured in a bunch of different ways. There’s even a leaderboard! The winners will include the person who shows the greatest difference between their chronological and biological age, as well as the person who manages to reverse their biological age the most.

The competition is the brainchild of the neuroscientist and physician Christin Glorioso, who is also founder and CEO of NeuroAge Therapeutics. The company offers tools to track brain health and aging and is running a trial to find out if biological brain age can predict the onset of Alzheimer’s disease.

Glorioso says she has several goals for the Younger contest. The first, she tells me, is to “explain to the world what aging clocks are.” Regular Checkup readers will be familiar with these tools, but for the uninitiated, they are basically designed to measure biological age.

Many measure chemical signatures that form a layer on top of our DNA and seem to change with age. But others might involve looking at proteins or lipids in blood. Some are designed to measure functional health, while others predict when a person will die. There are more than a hundred clocks out there, and they probably each capture a specific aspect of the biological process of aging.

These clocks are proving very useful for scientists, who use them to study aging and development in humans and many other species. But using them to estimate the biological age of an individual person is more controversial. They’re just not good enough for that yet.

Part of the problem is that we don’t really understand what each clock is capturing. Glorioso hopes that data collected through the Younger contest might help answer that question. She’s hoping to generate “the world’s most comprehensive clock dataset.”

Some longevity clinics try to get around the limits of biological age testing by using multiple clocks. That’s this competition’s approach too. As a standard competitor, I’ll be sending a blood spot sample to TruDiagnostic, a company that measures epigenetic chemical groups on DNA and offers to reveal an overall biological age as well as a person’s pace of aging and the biological ages of each of 11 organ systems, including the heart and brain.

I’ll get a brain age score from NeuroAge once I complete the cognitive tasks on offer. I’ll also submit some physical measures like grip strength. And I’ll upload a series of selfies to an app developed by a team at Harvard that promises to tell me my face age. That’s exactly what it sounds like—an estimate of how old my face looks.

I’m intrigued to see my scores, even though I know I shouldn’t put too much stock in them. The first time I took a test, four years ago, the company I used gave me a biological age that matched my chronological age, which was a little disappointing and, if I’m honest, a bit underwhelming. A year later, the same company told me I had a young heart but a relatively old brain, liver, and hormonal system. My lifestyle hasn’t changed much since then. Will the years have made much difference?

(Ultra competitors—who pay $4,499 rather than the $999 cost of regular entry—are also offered a range of other blood tests and clocks, as well as MRI and DEXA scans. I’ve got complimentary press access to the standard package.)

Glorioso is also hoping to gather information about the effects of some purported longevity approaches. During the competition, some participants will be offered red-light masks, access to a sauna, or other low-risk offerings that partner companies who are sponsoring the event to varying degrees might want to collect data on. “A lot of these companies just can’t afford to run [clinical] trials,” says Glorioso.

She also sees the event as a public health initiative. A couple of years ago, David Sinclair, who studies aging at Harvard Medical School, and his colleagues estimated that if we could slow down aging in the general population and increase life expectancy by one year, it would save the US economy $38 trillion.

Glorioso took her own baseline measurements back in August. Those initial tests suggested that her biological age was around 10 years below her chronological age. That sounded pretty impressive to me until I looked at the leaderboard and saw that competitor @Fred had a biological age 28.8 years below his chronological age.

The leaderboard is pretty sparse at the moment, as only seven people have logged their baseline measurements so far. Six of them have biological ages tracking low, but one 47-year-old has been given a biological age of 68.1. She’s competing publicly, so I can see the breakdown of her scores. The worst is for the speed at which she can stand from sitting in a chair—by that measure, she’s been given a biological age of 100.

Hillary Lin, a longevity-focused physician in New York, has just started logging her baseline measurements for the competition. She tells me she’s taken biological age tests in the past and that they’ve tended to give scores below her chronological age, which is currently 37. Last year, the TruDiagnostic test put her pace of aging at 0.75—suggesting she’s only doing nine months’ worth of aging in a typical year. “That’s supposed to be quite good,” she says.

If it had been up to her, Lin says, she would have incorporated more blood tests into the competition, to build a fuller picture of a person’s health. And she’s worried that a six-month period might not be long enough to see changes in biological measures of aging. Still, she’s excited, and is already making plans to

history.title: India pledged its gold and changed course
history.what: With foreign reserves down to about two weeks of imports, India physically flew 47 tonnes of gold to the Bank of England as collateral for an emergency loan. Within weeks the government devalued the rupee twice and began dismantling the licensing system that had governed Indian industry since independence.
history.why: Decades of import substitution had produced an economy that could not earn enough foreign exchange. The Gulf war spiked oil prices and cut remittances from Indians working in the Gulf simultaneously. The Soviet Union, a major trading partner, was collapsing. Political instability meant credit lines were pulled. Several slow problems arrived together with one fast shock — the usual anatomy of a crisis.
history.impact: The rupee fell about 20% in two days. Inflation hit 13%. But what followed was the most consequential economic change in modern Indian history: industrial licensing was abolished, import tariffs that reached 300% began falling, and foreign investment was allowed in.
history.policy: Liberalisation — of licensing, trade and investment — plus a managed floating rupee instead of a fixed one, and a deliberate policy of accumulating foreign exchange reserves so it could never happen again.
history.consequence: India's growth rate roughly doubled over the following two decades. The companies that dominate the Nifty today — the private banks, the IT exporters, the consumer giants — are largely creatures of the post-1991 settlement. And the reserve-hoarding instinct stuck: India now holds well over a year of import cover, which is why rupee wobbles since have been uncomfortable rather than existential.
history.pattern: Crises are when structural reform becomes politically possible. Changes that were unthinkable for forty years were passed in weeks because the alternative was default. The investment lesson is the flip side: the point of maximum fear is often the start of the best decade.
history.india_echo: This is the founding event of the market you invest in. Every time you read that foreign investors are selling, remember that they were only allowed to buy at all because of a fortnight in 1991 when the country nearly ran out of dollars.
history.watch_for: Import cover measured in months of reserves. It is the single number that separates a currency having a bad week from a country having a crisis.
